title: Asking a Crafty Question Upward Can Carry an Indirect Punch
author: Admired Leadership
summary: This article addresses the difficulty of giving upward feedback to a defensive boss, and proposes asking a curious question as a safer, indirect way to deliver the same message. It argues that any piece of feedback can be reframed as a genuine question about the leader's logic or strategy, which invites reflection instead of triggering defensiveness. A worked example shows an employee asking a leader who talks too much in meetings for advice on their own speaking-to-listening ratio, letting the leader draw the connection themselves. The piece stresses that the specific answer the leader gives doesn't matter; the act of posing the question is what plants the idea, and arguing over the response would undercut the strategy. The archivist notes this is a tactical, technique-based piece useful for readers managing up.
points: Direct criticism of a boss risks being read as insubordination, so feedback delivered as a genuine question is often safer.
Any piece of feedback can be reframed as a curious question about the leader's own logic or strategy.
A worked example shows how to surface a leader's overtalking in meetings by asking for their advice on your own behavior.
The leader's specific answer to the question is beside the point; posing the question itself delivers the feedback.
Arguing over the leader's response undermines the technique, so the best move is to let the question sit.
quotes: Giving the leader above you some candid feedback or criticism can prove to be a dicey proposition.
Unfortunately, the consequence of holding back means repeatedly enduring the same ineffective behaviors, messages, or choices.
Letting questions carry feedback is an indirect way to make a point without challenging others.
It really doesn’t matter what their answer is. The feedback has been delivered simply by asking the question.
Don’t ruin the influence it will have by arguing over whether the answer is accurate or to your liking.
Asking your leader to explain the logic, rationale, or strategy behind their choices simultaneously promotes that you want to learn from them.
